back: $x'=(x-\bar x)/\sigma$ gives mean 0, std 1; $x'=(x-\min)/(\max-\min)$ maps to $[0,1]$. Needed for distance- and gradient-based models, not for trees.
Split first. Fit every learned statistic (mean, std, median, vocabulary, selected features, encodings, thresholds) on the training split only; apply it unchanged to validation and test.

front: One-hot vs label vs target encoding
back: One-hot: m binary columns, no order, large for many categories. Label: one integer, false order. Target: category mean of y, powerful but leaks unless computed on train (out-of-fold).
Map each category string to one of $B$ buckets with a hash function. Fixed feature size, handles unseen categories; costs random collisions and interpretability.
Combine features into one categorical (e.g. 'Married, 2') to let linear models express interactions. Cardinalities multiply: $100\times100=10{,}000$ values.
Missing not at random (depends on the value itself), at random (depends on another observed variable), completely at random (no pattern, rare).
Impute with training median/mode and add a missingness indicator. Avoid deletion unless MCAR and tiny; avoid plausible fill values like 0 children.
Filter: score features without a model (variance, correlation, mutual information). Wrapper: search subsets with a model (RFE). Embedded: selection during training (L1, tree importance).

Random split of time data; scaling/imputing before splitting; duplicates across splits; group leakage; data-generation artefacts; selection or target encoding with test labels; features derived from the label.
Too-good scores, a single feature with extreme predictive power, big drop in ablation, big jump when adding a feature, repeated peeking at the test set.
Little signal for the rare class, a trivial majority-class solution that is hard to beat, and asymmetric error costs.
$w_c=N/(C\,n_c)$. With 950/50, the positive weight is 10 and the negative 0.526. Equivalent in expectation to oversampling, without duplicate rows.
Copy minority rows / drop majority rows / interpolate $x+u(x'-x)$ between minority neighbours. Do it after the split, on train only; never evaluate on resampled data.
Keep the model, change the cut-off: sweep it on validation data and pick the one maximising F1 or minimising expected cost. 0.5 is arbitrary under imbalance.
Divide posteriors by training class fractions, multiply by true fractions, renormalise (Bishop 1.5.4). 0.8 from a 50/50 model at 1% prevalence becomes 0.039.
